headline: A Large-Scale Study on Teachers’ Knowledge of Common Student Struggles in Mathematics
blurb: Teachers’ knowledge of common student struggles is widely recognized as a key component of teacher knowledge across subject areas. However, most large-scale research has focused on measuring teachers’ awareness of student struggles, with little attention paid to how teachers interpret their underlying reasons. This study examined 743 mathematics teachers’ knowledge of common student struggles with ratios and proportional relationships, an important content area in the middle school mathematics curriculum. Teachers were asked to identify the most common incorrect student solutions to eight mathematical tasks and to interpret the underlying reasons for these struggles. While many teachers demonstrated awareness of empirically documented common student struggles, they tended to attribute these struggles to procedural issues rather than to conceptual misunderstandings. Hierarchical logistic regression analyses indicated that teachers’ awareness of common student struggles and their own content knowledge were linked to how they interpreted students’ struggles.
authors: Li, J., Ezaki, J., & Copur-Gencturk, Y.

headline: Necessary but Not Sufficient: School Administrator Support and Teacher Safety, Anxiety/Stress, Retention, and Victimization
blurb: With growing concerns about school violence and teacher victimization in U.S. schools, it remains unclear if administrator support is enough to address teacher safety, anxiety and stress, and retention. Using a national sample of 5,550 pre-K–12th-grade teachers, we examined the effect of administrative support on retention intentions, the mediating effect of perceived safety and anxiety and stress, and how teacher victimization by students moderates associations between administrator support and teacher safety, anxiety and stress, and retention intentions. Path analysis revealed that administrator support related to retention intentions directly and indirectly through teacher safety and anxiety and stress. Teacher victimization by students moderated these relations such that higher rates of victimization weakened the relationship between administrator support and retention intentions.
authors: Perry, A. H., Reddy, L. A., Martinez, A., McMahon, S. D., Astor, R. A., Worrell, F. C., Anderman, E. M., & Espelage, D. L.

headline: Postsecondary Gaps in Recovery From the COVID-19 Pandemic: Evidence From Public Colleges and Universities
blurb: We study changes in postsecondary student performance during and after the COVID-19 pandemic using administrative data on all 2015–2022 high school graduates in North Carolina who enrolled in an in-state public institution. Successful course completion rates increased briefly at 4-year institutions at the start of the pandemic, but at both 2- and 4-year institutions, success rates and credit earning decreased for later cohorts. These declines have persisted for certain groups, including students from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups, economically disadvantaged and academically weaker students, as well as female students. The findings point to ongoing academic challenges faced by vulnerable college student populations in the postpandemic period.
authors: Gicheva, D., Edmunds, J. A., Hutchins, B. C., Eilam, N., & Arshavsky, N.

headline: Identifying Structural Inequity During COVID-19: Teachers’ Workload and Resources by Instructional Mode
blurb: The COVID-19 pandemic has disproportionately affected students in segregated Black and Latine communities, highlighting the need for equitable workload and resources for teachers to support these students effectively. Analyzing the 2020–2021 National Teacher and Principal Survey data and guided by a critical quantitative framework, we found that teachers in predominantly Black and Latine schools had heavier workloads and were given less adequate resources than their counterparts in predominantly White schools, especially when they were teaching hybrid. We also found that teachers with hybrid instruction in predominantly Black and Latine schools who received more adequate resources were less likely to be dissatisfied and express their intention to leave teaching. Policy and leadership implications in times of crisis are discussed.
authors: Akiba, M., Jiang, X., & Ikoma, S.

headline: Untapped Potential? Understanding the Paraeducator-to-Teacher Pipeline and Its Potential for Diversifying the Teacher Workforce
blurb: Paraeducators are among the largest categories of public education employees and are increasingly seen as a pool of potential teachers. However, little is known about paraeducator-to-teacher transitions. Using statewide administrative data, we show that while paraeducators may be more racially/ethnically diverse than the teacher workforce, Black and Hispanic paraeducators are less likely than White paraeducators to transition into teaching. We additionally show that teachers with paraeducator experience are similarly effective to teachers without paraeducator experience. Lastly, we use simulations to show that the potential for the paraeducator-to-teacher pipeline to diversify the teaching profession may be limited unless they are highly targeted. Our results have policy design implications for efforts to expand the paraeducator-to-teacher pipeline or to diversify the teacher workforce.
authors: Camp, A. M., Zamarro, G., & McGee, J. B.

headline: Bulwark or Barrier? The Effect of Academic Criteria-Based Reclassification on the High School Outcomes of Multilingual Learners in Texas
blurb: English learner (EL) classification can provide multilingual students (MLs) with key supports while limiting access to important educational opportunities. To determine when students are ready to exit EL status, some states require students to meet academic criteria in addition to demonstrated English proficiency. However, few studies empirically examine these criteria, which may become increasingly restrictive in upper grades. We use administrative data from Texas and a regression discontinuity (RD) design to estimate the effect of using academic criteria to reclassify students at the end of eighth grade. Reclassified students earn more advanced credits, but graduate high school at lower rates, indicating a need for greater course access for EL-classified students and increased support for former ML-ELs.
authors: Xu, S. H., Flanagan, C., & Quintero, D.

headline: Changing Buses: Commute Complexity and Academic Outcomes
blurb: This study exploits a major overhaul of the public transportation system to examine the relationship between commute difficulty and academic outcomes. Specifically, we use administrative data from all high school students in the Baltimore City Public Schools during the 2016–17 and 2017–18 school years to compare the school mobility rates, attendance, and grade point averages of cohorts of students right before and after the overhaul. We use route fixed effects to compare students to their neighbors and classmates who would have had the same estimated commute to school if not for the system-wide changes in routes and schedules. Total travel time does not predict any of our outcomes, but we find that students in years when the commute required a bus transfer are more likely to change schools and to be absent. These findings imply that districts should prioritize direct routes to school for students whenever possible.
authors: Burdick-Will, J., & Stein, M. L.

headline: Sorting the Principal Pipeline: Subject-Area Pathways and Career Mobility in School Leadership
blurb: Using longitudinal administrative data from Texas spanning nearly three decades and following more than one million educators, this study finds educators who become principals follow relatively direct pathways, and that subject-area specialization (ELA, social studies, STEM, elementary) shapes who advances, operating as a career-mobility sorting system.
authors: Pendola, A.

headline: The Decline of Adult Education: Supply, Demand, and Public Support for Immigrant-Serving Educational Services
blurb: Public adult education enrollment fell from nearly 2.7 million (2000) to under 1.3 million (2023). As demand for basic-skills training from native-born adults declined and demand for English instruction from immigrants rose, the growing immigrant share appears to have lowered public willingness to invest, constraining supply.
authors: Heller, B. H., & Slungaard Mumma, K.

headline: Pathways and Outcomes for Early-Career Teachers With Teaching Assistant Experience
blurb: North Carolina's teaching assistant (TA)-to-teacher pipeline: teachers with prior TA experience make up a meaningful share of beginners, are more likely to be people of color and teach special education, perform comparably to peers, and are much more likely to stay in teaching.
authors: Bastian, K. C., Fuller, S. C., Otte, A., & Mikkelsen, C.

headline: Teacher Sorting and Preferences over School Disadvantage: Evidence from Performance Pay in Texas
blurb: In this paper I study how performance-based compensation affects teacher mobility and sorting using the Texas Teacher Incentive Allotment (TIA), a statewide program introduced in 2019. TIA gives teachers a tiered quality designation, Recognized, Exemplary, or Master, based on performance evaluations and value-added measures. These designations are portable across schools and come with a salary…
authors: Patrick L. Massey

headline: The Labor Market Value of Community College Bachelor's Degrees: Initial Evidence from a Resume Audit Study in Early Childhood Education
blurb: Community colleges are more financially, academically, and geographically accessible than four-year institutions. Yet despite most community college students intending to earn a bachelor's degree, few successfully transfer and complete one. Community College Baccalaureate (CCB) programs have emerged as an alternative pathway, allowing community colleges to confer bachelor's degrees directly. However, little is known about how employers value these credentials in the labor market. To address this question, we conduct the first resume audit study of CCB degrees…
authors: Riley K. Acton, Camila Morales, Julia A. Turner, Lois Miller, Kalena Cortes

authors: Audrey Boochever

headline: Course Failure in Dual Enrollment and the Impact on College-Going

This study examines the characteristics of students who fail dual enrollment, the consequences of failure, and whether attempting DE retains value even for students who do not succeed. Using administrative data…
authors: Jenna Howard Terrell, Joanna Rometsch Mathias, Diana Roldan-Rueda, Alyssa Blanchard

headline: Family Language Transmission Under Institutional Language Regimes Shapes Adolescent Mental Health Through Peers
blurb: In many societies, institutional languages shape participation, recognition, and belonging, while families transmit language backgrounds across generations. These inherited backgrounds may contribute to children's communication and, once children enter shared peer environments, to the experiences of their classmates. I show evidence that family language backgrounds travel across households…

headline: The Maternal Labor Market Effects of State Pre-K Funding
blurb: Public pre-kindergarten (pre-K) is primarily designed as an educational policy for young children but has attracted attention as a potential lever to support maternal employment. This study provides national evidence on the maternal labor market effects of state pre-K funding, exploiting variation in public investment across states and over time (academic years 2002-2024)…
authors: Eunho Cha, Mindy L. Rosengarten, Tyler W. Watts, Kenneth A. Dodge, Jade M. Jenkins

This study employs a multi-method analysis of the Near North Side Choice Neighborhoods Initiative (CNI) in St. Louis, Missouri, the nation's largest mixed-income redevelopment program…
authors: Jason Jabbari, Andrew Foell, DeMarcus Jenkins, Yung Chun, Odis Johnson Jr.

headline: Career and Technical Education as a Strategy to Improve Long-term Outcomes for English Language Learners
blurb: Career and Technical Education (CTE) has emerged as a strategy to enhance college and labor market outcomes for all students, yet little is known about its implications for multilingual students classified as English Learners (ML-ELs). Using longitudinal data from Massachusetts, this study provides some of the first evidence on ML-ELs' CTE participation and its relationship with long-term…
authors: Coral Flanagan, Shaun M. Dougherty

headline: Compounded Disadvantage: Intersectional Inequities in Chronic Absenteeism Prevalence and Recovery During the COVID-19 Era

Consistent with national evidence, chronic absenteeism roughly doubled from prepandemic levels…
authors: Jerome Graham, Richard O. Welsh, Su Yon Choi

headline: Neighborhood Effects and Missing Markets for Opportunity
blurb: Experimental and quasi-experimental studies show that childhood neighborhoods have substantial causal impacts on children's adult earnings and other long-term socioeconomic outcomes. Several market failures are likely to lead to excessive residential segregation by parental income and to an under-supply of mixed-income neighborhoods…
authors: Lawrence F. Katz

headline: ERC Explains: A Guide to Senate Bill 2 and Texas Education Freedom Accounts

headline: Economics of Encouragement: Can a Single Email Shape What Students Study?
blurb: A student's choice of college major significantly influences their long-term career outcomes and earning potential. Despite this, many qualified students do not consider certain fields due to a lack of encouragement or suggestion. This brief summarizes a research study in Economics of Education Review that examines whether sending a short, supportive email from a professor can influence students' course enrollment and major decisions. The study analyzed data from over 10,000 students enrolled in a large introductory economics course at Texas A&M University. High-performing students received an email from their professor commending their academic performance and encouraging further study in economics. Receipt of the email increased the likelihood of enrolling in the next economics course, with the effect being largest for first-generation and underrepresented students.
authors: Olivia Edwards, Jonathan Meer

headline: Equity in Practice: How New Teachers Bring Fairness Into the Classroom
blurb: Classrooms in the United States serve students a broader range of backgrounds than in previous decades, and teachers are increasingly expected to provide instruction that is fair and responsive to all students. However, limited evidence exists regarding whether new teachers are adequately prepared to achieve this in practice. This brief summarizes a research study in The Urban Review that examines how beginning teachers describe their efforts to account for students' cultural, racial, and linguistic backgrounds. Researchers analyzed nearly 1,900 survey responses from new teachers participating in one of California's largest teacher induction programs. Only a small proportion described their teaching in terms that reflected a clear focus on equity. However, those who did provided detailed accounts of how beginning teachers can incorporate fairness into their classrooms, outlining a progression from including diverse voices to addressing systemic inequities. The study identifies specific practices that teacher preparation and support programs can implement to help more new teachers develop these capacities.
authors: Andrew Kwok, Jenna Davis, Sara Halabi, Joseph Waddington, Debbee Huston, Rita Hemsley

headline: Managing without Mandate: A Nationwide Review of State Training Laws
blurb: Managing student behavior is a persistent challenge in teaching, yet teacher preparation programs often devote limited attention to this area. Classroom and behavior management (CBM) means equipping teachers to create environments that support both academic learning and positive behavior. When teachers do not receive adequate preparation, they are more likely to use punitive or exclusionary discipline, which disproportionately affects students of color. This brief summarizes a research study in Education Finance and Policy that examines what state laws require regarding support for classroom and behavior management. Reviewing discipline-related statutes from all 50 states and the District of Columbia (drawn from a 5,207-page national compendium), the study found only 31 statutes in 21 states that specifically address support for general classroom teachers. Most identify who provides training and which staff are included, but few specify whether training is required or how often it should occur.
authors: Megan Svajda-Hardy, Andrew Kwok

headline: Property Tax Salience and Public Good Investment: Evidence from School Bond Elections
blurb: In 2019, Texas passed legislation requiring that the ballot text for all school bond referenda include the phrase "THIS IS A PROPERTY TAX INCREASE," highlighting property taxes as their primary funding mechanism. Evaluating the impact of this policy change on voter behavior in a difference-in-differences framework, we find that the introduction of property tax disclaimers reduced the passage rate of school bonds by approximately 9 percentage points relative to other municipal bonds, which were unaffected by the policy. The effects are driven by November elections, where less-informed voters may be more influenced by ballot language. Two survey experiments reinforce our finding that property tax disclaimers increase the salience of property taxes, erode support for school bonds, and shift attention away from the benefits of bonds. When bonds are projected to substantially increase property tax obligations, Texas-style property tax disclaimers reduce voter errors, but for bonds with small impacts on property taxes, these disclaimers increase voter errors.
authors: Blake H. Heller, Melissa Arnold Lyon

headline: Immigration Enforcement Actions and Empty Desks: Persistent and Acute Attendance Effects
blurb: How do immigration enforcement actions (IEAs) affect student attendance, and through what channels? We use student-by-day administrative records from a mid-size school district to estimate the causal effect of heightened federal immigration enforcement following the January 2025 presidential inauguration on student attendance using a difference-in-differences design. We find that IEAs cause a substantial and persistent increase in absences among foreign-born students, with the daily probability of absence rising by 2.2 percentage points (37%) relative to a pre-treatment mean of 5.9%. We decompose these effects into two distinct channels: 1. a sustained elevation in absences spanning the full post-treatment period and 2. acute, short-lived spikes on dates proximate to specific enforcement events. The sustained elevation in absences dominates and show no signs of attenuation during our study period. Effects increase nearly monotonically with grade level, consistent with older students exercising greater autonomy over their own attendance decisions. We also show that estimates using more common proxies for student vulnerability, such as MLL status, likely understate the effects experienced by the most directly affected students.
authors: Andrew Camp, Jonathon Acosta, Janelle Haire, Edom Tesfa

headline: AI in PK-12 Education: Implications for Teaching and Learning
blurb: This research and policy review from the Metropolitan Educational Research Consortium (MERC) explores the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) for teaching and learning in public PK-12 education. It is part of a two part series with a companion report focused on AI implications for PK-12 policy. The report explores two questions: 1. How is AI shaping teaching and instructional practice? 2. How is AI shaping student learning and development? It concludes with a series of key takeaways and recommendations for PK-12 policy and practice.
authors: David Naff, Meleah Ellison, Casey Bailey, Tzu-Wei Wang, Kiana Bradford

headline: Trends in Local Teacher Supply Since the COVID-19 Pandemic: Evidence from Teacher Job Applications
blurb: Recent survey evidence documents pandemic-era challenges in filling teacher vacancies and hiring from too-small applicant pools. However, direct evidence quantifying changes in teacher supply since the onset of the pandemic is scarce. Using longitudinal teacher job application data from a large southeastern school district, we examine trends in local teacher supply from 2015 to 2023. We find substantial declines in the number of applications per job posting beginning in 2021, with application rates 52% to 75% lower than pre-pandemic projections. These declines are pervasive across both hard-to-staff and easier-to-staff subjects, as well as across higher- and lower-poverty schools. We also document that the new teacher applicant pool was 23% to 31% smaller than pre-pandemic projections during this period. These findings advance our understanding of current teacher staffing challenges and underscore the need for research in additional contexts to establish the broader prevalence of these declines.
authors: Olivia L. Chi, Elc Estrera, Matthew A. Lenard

headline: Teacher Certification in Texas: District Strategies to Recruit and Retain a Credentialed Workforce
blurb: Texas faces persistently high teacher attrition and declining enrollment in university-based preparation programs. Between 2019–20 and 2024–25, the share of uncertified teachers (i.e., teachers without any state certification) more than tripled. Despite this statewide surge, district-level certification rates varied considerably across contexts, with some districts maintaining high teacher certification rates. Interviewed leaders, from districts selected for having high certification rates and/or noted success in supporting the certification process, highlighted key strategies to prioritize certification: (1) preparation partnerships to increase the pipeline of new certified teachers, (2) prioritization of certification in recruitment and hiring practices, (3) salary incentives along with tracking and dedicated staff to support uncertified teachers toward certification, and (4) retention of new teachers through mentoring and specific supports. House Bill 2, landmark legislation passed by the Texas legislature in 2025, offers districts unprecedented financial investments in recruitment, preparation, certification, and mentoring that can increase the rate of certified teachers.
authors: Susan Kemper Patrick, Chazz Higginbotham, Ryan Saunders, Tiffany S. Tan, Steve Wojcikiewicz

headline: The Effects of High-Impact Tutoring on Student Attendance: Evidence from a State Initiative
blurb: Student absenteeism surged during and after the pandemic, harming engagement and achievement. We evaluate the impact of Washington DC's High-Impact Tutoring (HIT) Initiative, designed to mitigate learning loss through targeted academic supports, on student absenteeism. Using daily attendance data and a within-student fixed effects design, we find that students were 1.2 percentage points less likely to be absent on days they were scheduled for tutoring, a 7.0% reduction. Bundling key features of high-impact tutoring, such as in-school delivery, smaller tutor–student ratios, and increased frequency of sessions, further amplify the effect. These results highlight HIT's potential to boost engagement while promoting equitable access to supportive learning environments.
authors: Monica G. Lee, Susanna Loeb, Carly D. Robinson

headline: Identifying Effective Attendance Strategies in Michigan
blurb: Chronic absenteeism remains a persistent challenge in Michigan and across the country in the years following the COVID-19 pandemic (Singer, 2024). While schools have expanded their efforts to improve attendance (Singer & Lenhoff, 2025), there is still limited evidence about which of these strategies are most effective in improving student attendance. In particular, it remains difficult to disentangle the role of school-based efforts from the broader social and economic conditions that shape attendance, which makes it challenging to identify which strategies are most likely to make a difference. This report provides new evidence on the relationship between school attendance strategies and student attendance outcomes in Michigan. We use longitudinal administrative data to construct a school-level attendance value-added measure, which isolates schools' contributions to student attendance after accounting for differences in student populations and contexts. We then use survey data from school leaders to examine how variation in attendance practices, organizational systems, staffing, and leadership corresponds with differences in attendance value-added across schools. This approach allows us to examine the extent to which various strategies are associated with positive attendance outcomes.
authors: Jeremy Singer, Sarah Winchell Lenhoff, Angela Lyle

headline: Improving Student Achievement: What Red, Blue, and Purple States Are Doing Right

Speakers include Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont, Colorado Commissioner Susana Córdova, Maryland Superintendent Carey M. Wright, Sydnee Dickson, and Linda Darling-Hammond. Useful for anyone tracking how states build coherent systems rather than one-off reforms.

headline: Postsecondary Pathways: Aligning Education, Correctional Rehabilitation, and Workforce Readiness
blurb: Education and vocational training inside correctional facilities is associated with a 43% drop in the odds of returning to prison, along with better employment after release. This webinar looks at how long-term education and labor data can be used to design prison education and reentry programs that line up with real job openings in high-demand industries.

headline: Investing in Educators, Improving Families' Access to Care: Evidence from DC's Early Educator Compensation Initiative
blurb: Since 2022, the District of Columbia's Office of the State Superintendent of Education (OSSE) has used tax revenue to raise early educator wages on a salary scale tied to role and education. Urban Institute researchers, who have studied the program with OSSE since its start, will present new evidence on workforce retention and families' access to affordable, higher-quality care, plus takeaways for policymakers elsewhere.

headline: Expanding the Reach and Impact of School Meals: How and Why Do Changes to the Community Eligibility Provision Affect Adoption?
blurb: A decade of shifts in the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), which lets high-poverty schools serve free meals to all students, shows that lowering the eligibility threshold did little on its own: only 7 percent of newly eligible schools adopted in year one. Medicaid data matching raised eligibility metrics by about 6 percentage points, and adopting districts gained an average of $42.48 per pupil in federal funding. Rural districts faced the steepest costs.
authors: Emily Gutierrez, Ariella Meltzer, Erin Hysom

headline: Estimating the Overall Effects of Statewide Early Literacy Policies: Evidence from Michigan
source: Annenberg Institute at Brown University, EdWorkingPapers
blurb: Michigan's statewide early literacy reform raised third-grade reading achievement by 8.7 percent of a standard deviation, using a synthetic difference-in-differences design. Gains were larger for cohorts exposed longer, persisted past third grade, and came without more grade retention or effects on math. The authors benchmark Michigan against South Carolina, where gains were smaller, and Mississippi, where they were larger.
authors: Seth Walker, Josep M. Nadal-Fernandez, Tara Kilbride

headline: The Effects of State-Level Loan Forgiveness Policies on Teacher Supply
blurb: State loan forgiveness programs for teachers raise first-year enrollment in education preparation programs by about 12 percent, but show no overall effect on total enrollment or bachelor's degrees awarded, according to a difference-in-differences analysis. The degree result masks variation by how much debt is forgiven. Moran cautions that gains are small relative to staffing needs and require sizable state investment.
authors: Alex J Moran

headline: The Role of Career Advising in High School in Shaping the Aspirations of First-Generation Students
source: EdWorkingPapers, Annenberg Institute at Brown University
blurb: Using 2018 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) data from the United States and Costa Rica, this paper asks whether who delivers high school career advising (counselors or teachers) and how it is scheduled (formal or voluntary) shifts first-generation students' college aspirations. Neither factor showed a significant association. Aspiration gaps persisted in both countries and were wider in the United States, pointing to structural barriers over delivery design.
authors: Catherine Mata

headline: Translating Policy into Opportunity: School Counselors and the Implementation of CTE-Focused Dual Enrollment Pathways
source: Annenberg Institute at Brown University, EdWorkingPapers
topic: Dual enrollment and career and technical education
blurb: Tennessee has invested heavily in dual enrollment at its technical colleges, but who gets in depends heavily on the local high school. Drawing on surveys of 1,382 Tennessee College of Applied Technology students and 510 counselors plus focus groups with 44 counselors, the study finds recruitment models vary widely, counselors carry heavier advising and administrative loads than for academic dual enrollment, and students report gains in self-efficacy and college-going behavior.
authors: Nicole Mader, Stone Dawson, JoHanna Sestito, Raven Powell, Kaitlyn Dodgen, Victoria Harpool

headline: 23 Years of State Pre-K Expansion: How States Balance Investment, Access, and Quality in the Modern Era
blurb: State-funded pre-kindergarten (pre-K) grew sharply between 2002 and 2024, and this descriptive study finds a 200% enrollment increase came alongside a 21% average rise in per-pupil spending rather than thinner funding. Universal-eligibility states enrolled more children in state programs, but overall preschool enrollment, including private options, was similar to means-tested states.
authors: Casey Moran, Mindy L. Rosengarten, Eunho Cha, Jade M. Jenkins, Kenneth A. Dodge, Allison Friedman-Kraus, W. Steven Barnett, Tyler W. Watts

headline: No Pay? No Way! Teacher Compensation Reforms and the Market for Graduate Degrees
blurb: Tennessee's move to end the salary premium teachers earned for graduate credentials cut enrollment in education graduate fields by 27 percent, roughly 140 students, with the sharpest declines at non-research-intensive universities. Lost enrollment also trimmed tuition revenue and related state funding. Useful for anyone weighing how kindergarten through grade 12 pay reform reverberates through teacher preparation programs and public higher education budgets.
authors: Taylor Odle, Patrick Delgado

headline: Discipline Beyond Suspensions: Racial/Ethnic Disparities Across the Spectrum of Disciplinary Actions
blurb: Detailed administrative records from a large southern district show that school leaders usually respond to an incident with a single punitive action rather than guidance-based supports, and that non-exclusionary alternatives are themselves applied unevenly. Among students in the same fight, White students more often lost privileges as the harshest consequence, while Black students more often received suspensions or referrals to a school resource officer.
authors: Youngsun Lee, Jing Liu, Emily K. Penner

headline: Teacher Localness, Early-Career Effectiveness, and Retention
source: Annenberg Institute at Brown University, EdWorkingPapers
blurb: Statewide Maryland data test whether "Grow-Your-Own" logic holds up: do teachers with local roots do better? Certification pathway, not localness, best predicts early-career effectiveness, with university-prepared teachers outperforming conditionally certified peers in math by 0.06 standard deviations. Local upbringing and local training instead predict staying in the same school or district, suggesting local recruitment complements rather than replaces strong preparation.
authors: Nicolas Dominguez-Mel, Wesley T. Morris, Sarah Montana, David Blazar

headline: Where Have All the Zeros Gone? The Landscape of No Zeros Grading Policies
source: CALDER Center (Center for Analysis of Longitudinal Data in Education Research)
blurb: No-zeros policies (NZPs) bar teachers from giving zeros on assignments or course grades, and adoption in Washington State more than doubled over the past decade, from about 30 districts in 2015-16 to nearly 70 in 2024-25. The authors build a typology of how these policies are written and communicated, and find NZPs are less common in districts serving more low-income students.
authors: Dan Goldhaber, Maia Goodman Young, Luke Caldwell

headline: Teacher Effectiveness in Remote Instruction
blurb: Using matched student-teacher data from three large metro-Atlanta districts, this study estimates value-added models to compare teacher effectiveness before and during virtual instruction in 2020-21. Variation in effectiveness widened during remote teaching, driven by K-2 and middle school teachers. Veteran teachers fared relatively better than less experienced peers, while the strongest in-person teachers were most likely to see large declines.
authors: M. Cade Lawson, Tim R. Sass

headline: Geographic Disparities in Availability of Secondary Advanced STEM Coursework: Exploring Advanced Placement® Course Offerings Across the United States
topic: Rural access to advanced STEM coursework
blurb: Rural and town high schools offer fewer Advanced Placement (AP) science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) courses than their peers, and the gaps are widest for math-intensive subjects. The study joins the full set of AP course audit records from 2015 to 2019 with National Center for Education Statistics data on 21,139 public high schools, and maps how availability varies by region and locale.
authors: Kelly L. Boles

headline: Writing skills are getting more attention in school
blurb: With few states testing writing and no national elementary writing results published since 2002, districts such as Colorado's Douglas County report rising scores after training teachers in structured, research-backed writing instruction.

headline: Education researchers warn political review of federal grants could reshape what gets studied
blurb: Education research organizations warn that a proposed OMB overhaul of federal grant rules, adding review by political appointees, could narrow the questions researchers study and disrupt education studies already underway.

headline: In bipartisan rebuke, Senate panel votes to shield special ed from RFK Jr.'s agency
blurb: The Senate education committee voted 13-9, with two Republicans joining Democrats, to keep special education and other core offices within the Education Department amid the administration's effort to dismantle the agency.

headline: America's Colleges Are Hurtling Toward an Enrollment Cliff
blurb: The pipeline of traditional college-age students is entering a long decline, with U.S. high school graduates projected to fall roughly 13% through 2041 after peaking in 2025.

headline: Settling Scores: Experts Debate Why AP Performance Has Soared
blurb: The share of students earning passing scores on popular AP exams rose from 52% in 2021 to 71% in 2025, fueling debate over the College Board's revised scoring methodology.

headline: Head Start Could Soon Be Overhauled. Here's Exactly What Would Change.
blurb: A proposed federal rule would eliminate more than 1,400 regulatory provisions governing Head Start, including teacher-student ratios and bilingual instruction requirements, changes providers say would fundamentally reshape the 60-year-old program.

headline: A Bad Jobs Report for Public Education
blurb: Bureau of Labor Statistics data show K-12 schools shed 50,000 jobs from June to July and employ about 29,000 fewer workers than a year earlier, the first year-over-year decline since the pandemic.

headline: How a Years-Long Rise in Teacher Turnover Reshaped American Classrooms
blurb: An analysis spanning 21 states finds most experienced four to five consecutive years of elevated teacher turnover after 2020, with Texas losing 35,000 more teachers than pre-pandemic rates would have predicted.

headline: Outdoor Ed Programs Canceled for Tens of Thousands of Students After Federal Cuts
blurb: Federal funding cuts, including nearly $400 million in AmeriCorps grants, forced the cancellation of outdoor education programs for tens of thousands of students, including trips for nearly 24,000 in Maryland.

headline: When Teachers Lack Confidence in Math, Their Students Fall Behind, New Study Shows
blurb: A study of more than 3,000 Indiana teachers finds students score about one percentile lower when taught by math-anxious teachers, who are disproportionately assigned to low-income and struggling students.

headline: 15 states have laws that allow corporal punishment in schools. Here's where, and why
blurb: An NPR analysis finds 15 states still allow corporal punishment in schools, with federal data showing nearly 32,000 reported instances in 2021-22, concentrated almost entirely in eight mostly Southern states.

headline: University of Michigan won't use letter grades for some freshmen next fall
blurb: Starting in fall 2027, University of Michigan freshmen in its largest college will receive pass or no-credit marks instead of first-semester letter grades under a pilot aimed at easing academic pressure.

headline: As the only Texas district to trigger potential state takeover, Austin ISD's future now in TEA's hands
blurb: Two Austin middle schools received their fifth consecutive F ratings from the Texas Education Agency, triggering mandatory state intervention that could range from campus closures to a full district takeover.

headline: Race, Nativity, and the Labor Market Returns to College Major–Occupation Alignment
blurb: This study investigates the relationship between college major choices and labor market outcomes, with particular attention to racial minorities and immigrants. Building on research on major–occupation alignment, we focus on two dimensions: linkage, the extent to which majors are concentrated in specific occupations in the labor market, and match, whether individuals work in occupations closely related to their majors. Using American Community Survey data, we find that earning bachelor’s degrees in majors with strong linkage is associated with higher earnings—particularly for workers in matched occupations—and lower unemployment.
authors: Brian Holzman, Jeehee Han, Bethany Lewis, Irina Chukhray

headline: Classroom Composition Affects Teacher Performance Ratings
blurb: Teacher evaluations should reflect teaching performance rather than the characteristics of the students assigned to a teacher. Exploiting naturally occurring year-to-year variation in classroom composition within teachers, this article examines whether teacher performance ratings assigned by evaluators and students are influenced by classroom context. We find that teachers with higher-achieving and less disruptive students, holding constant the teacher and school, receive systematically higher performance ratings.
authors: William Delgado, Lauren Sartain

headline: Artificial Intelligence and the Teaching Workforce: Evidence From National Survey Data in the United States
blurb: Artificial intelligence (AI) has shifted rapidly from speculative innovation to active policy concern in U.S. education, yet nationally representative evidence on teachers’ capacity and well-being remains limited. Using U.S.
authors: Lei Jiang

headline: Causal Benefits of Arts Education for Students with Disabilities
source: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
blurb: Employing administrative data from a randomized controlled trial of 42 elementary and middle public schools, we investigate the causal effects of Houston’s Arts Access Initiative for the population of K-8 students receiving special education services. We find that substantially increasing arts learning opportunities in under-resourced schools led to fewer disciplinary infractions, improved attendance, and higher writing scores on standardized tests for students with disabilities. We find no evidence that increased arts instruction crowds out achievement in tested subjects, alleviating concerns that reallocating time toward the arts undermines performance in core academic areas.
authors: Brian Kisida, Daniel H. Bowen

headline: Tracking Inequality: Teachers and the Allocation of Educational Opportunities
blurb: Professionals routinely make consequential decisions for others without systematically observing how those decisions turn out. Whether such decisions reflect accurate forecasting or systematically distorted beliefs has important implications for equality of opportunity. We study this question in the context of teachers' recommendations for high school tracks by combining nationwide administrative data, randomized vignette experiments, belief elicitation, and a field experiment. Holding students' academic performance and interests constant, teachers are significantly less likely to recommend demanding academic tracks when students come from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds. This differential treatment is accompanied by systematically inaccurate beliefs: teachers substantially overestimate the probability that high-achieving disadvantaged students will fail in academically demanding schools. We then provide teachers with personalized feedback on their previous recommendations and objective information on the realized success of disadvantaged students. The intervention substantially reduces socioeconomic gaps in recommendations for high-achieving students. Effects are concentrated among boys assigned to teachers with the largest prior recommendation gaps and the most inaccurate beliefs. Among the high-achieving disadvantaged boys most affected by the intervention, these changes translate into higher enrollment in demanding academic tracks, without detectable adverse effects on short-run academic performance.
authors: Michela Carlana, Francesca Miserocchi, Eleonora Patacchini

headline: What Explains Support for Race-Related Topics in the Curriculum? Evidence From the Understanding America Study
blurb: Race-related content in the school curriculum is a subject of renewed political and policy attention. But what racial topics do Americans support students learning about, and what racial beliefs predict their views? This article reports on a large probability-based survey of American households on these topics. We find opposition to most racial topics in elementary schools and support in high schools as well as large partisan gaps on many specific topics. Certain attitudinal items—most notably valuing diverse contributions and concern about White students feeling guilty—are strongly predictive of partisan gaps. These findings provide much needed light for a debate that has animated substantial political controversy in recent years, suggesting paths forward for a more inclusive curriculum.

headline: Retaining Beginning Teachers: The Moderating Role of the Frequency and Teacher-Perceived Quality of Professional Development
blurb: Alternative certification (AC) programs are adopted to address teacher shortages, yet high turnover undermines workforce stability and educational equity. Using a national sample, this study examined how dimensions of in-service support relate to turnover intentions. Regression results revealed that a preparation gap in leaving intentions emerged among teachers with limited support. Crucially, regular (monthly or weekly) mentoring or coaching was associated with a reduction in this disparity. Additionally, higher perceived professional development quality was uniformly associated with reduced moving and leaving intentions for all teachers. Targeted professional support is a vital policy lever to promote a more sustainable teacher workforce.

headline: Expanding the Case for Student–Teacher Race/Ethnicity Matching: Implications for Students with Disabilities and English Learners
blurb: A large and growing body of research demonstrates the benefits of assigning students to teachers who share their racial or ethnic backgrounds. These benefits range from improved test scores and attendance to reduced suspension rates and higher graduation and college enrollment rates. Yet much of this evidence has been limited to the general student population. Our recent studies extend this literature by focusing on two student groups often overlooked in research and policy: students with disabilities and English learners. Taken together, the evidence underscores the need for educational researchers and policy makers to consider not just broad teacher diversity efforts, but also the targeted importance of race-matching—and in some cases language-matching—for students facing additional systemic barriers.

headline: Rethinking Rigor: High School Coursework and the Path to Postsecondary Success
topic: High School Coursework and Postsecondary Success
blurb: This study investigates whether rigorous coursework benefits all students or mainly those with strong preparation and motivation. Using nationally representative HSLS:09 data, we find that coursework intensity is associated with greater college enrollment, selective college attendance, and STEM major selection. These gains extend to students with lower academic performance, lower motivation, and disabilities. Low-SES students experience larger college attendance gains, while high-SES students benefit more in selective admissions and STEM fields. Gender differences show higher selective college enrollment for females and greater STEM participation for males. Racial disparities persist, but coursework intensity is positively linked to postsecondary success across groups.

headline: Raising the Floor: Teacher Retention Effects of a Statewide Minimum Salary Increase
blurb: Attracting and retaining a high-quality teacher workforce is a central challenge for education policy, and higher teacher salaries are often proposed as a solution. The LEARNS Act increased Arkansas's minimum teacher salary from $36,000 to $50,000, guaranteed all teachers a minimum raise of $2,000, and provided school districts with the flexibility to deviate from traditional, seniority-based salary schedules. We collected districts' teacher salary schedules one year before and after implementation and integrated these data with administrative records to study districts’ adjustment to the law and teacher retention during the first three years of the reform. We find that districts made the minimum adjustments necessary to meet the new requirements. These changes increased the competitiveness of starting salaries across districts and reduced salary variation statewide. The Act also substantially increased salaries in rural and high-poverty districts, weakening the negative relationship between starting salaries, student poverty, and rurality. Using a triple-difference design, we find that teachers who received raises exceeding the $2,000 minimum were more likely to remain in their districts, with the strongest retention effects among those receiving the largest increases. We also find evidence that these effects may fade as inflation erodes the real value of the initial salary gains.

headline: The Regulation of Charter Schools: National Patterns and Causal Effects
blurb: There is considerable debate and evidence about how governments should regulate contractors and other firms, but little on how government should regulate schools. In the first phase of this study, we focus on the correlation between indices of state charter school policies and measures of charter quantity (market share) and three measures of quality: statewide student achievement growth from the Center for Research on Education Outcomes (CREDO), closure of low-performing charter schools, and charter entry into low-performing school districts. States with no charter caps, multiple charter authorizers, and stronger contract renewal standards have higher charter market shares. We also see some evidence of a quality-quantity trade-off, so that increasing the number of charter schools is associated with reduced quality. The positive correlation between charter market share and the number of charter authorizers motivates a follow-up causal analysis. Using difference-in-differences analysis, we find evidence that adding a statewide authorizing body increased the statewide charter market share and the share of charter students from low-income households.

headline: School District Superintendents’ Leadership of Early Childhood Education: A National Survey
blurb: Early education programs are increasingly under the purview of public school districts. This study analyzes a nationally distributed survey of superintendents ( N = 404) from the National Longitudinal Superintendent Database to examine (a) superintendent beliefs about the importance of Pre-K, (b) district prioritization of Pre-K, (c) how districts structure Pre-K leadership, and (d) practices supporting Pre-K and early education. Findings show that superintendents have limited direct experience or formal training in early childhood education, strongly value Pre-K for promoting kindergarten readiness, generally support Pre-K but with varying prioritization, and often embed Pre-K leadership within broader administrative roles. These findings point to directions for future research and highlight policy and practice changes to strengthen superintendent leadership for early education in districts.

headline: How Do School Choice and Boundary Policies Shape School Segregation in the 100 Largest School Districts?
blurb: Racial and ethnic segregation persists in US public schools, and state and district policies on school choice and attendance boundaries shape how students are sorted among them. This data tool examines how those policies relate to segregation in the 100 largest school districts (excluding New York City). Researchers reviewed each district's website to score boundary-drawing transparency on a 1 to 5 scale, catalogued state open enrollment policies, and measured segregation using the Education Opportunity Project's normalized exposure index. Most districts sit in states with some open enrollment option (86 of 100), and most publish a formal boundary review process (66 of 100). Segregation averaged 0.21 on a 0 to 1 scale, highest for White-Black segregation (0.27). Districts with similar policies show a wide range of segregation levels, and transparent, participatory boundary processes do not necessarily increase integration. How leaders design and combine policies, and how those interact with state and local context, matters more than any single policy
authors: Jay Carter, Shana Metcalf, Ariella Meltzer, Emily Gutierrez

headline: When Counties Invest in Early Childhood
blurb: The authors evaluated the implementation of the Early Childhood Impact Fund (ECIF) in Harris County, Texas. ECIF provided $15 million to programs serving children from birth to age 5, their caregivers, and early childhood professionals.

headline: Under the Weather? Seasonal Effects of Temperature on Student Test Performance
blurb: As students are exposed to extreme temperatures with ever-increasing frequency, it is important to understand how such exposure affects student performance. Drawing on detailed Measures of Academic Progress (MAP) achievement data combined with high-resolution weather records, we estimate the effect of temperature on student test performance across a six-year period for students in Tulsa, Oklahoma… more →
authors: Deven Carlson, Adam Shepardson

headline: What Drives Special Education Spending: Evidence from Texas School Districts
blurb: Special education finance systems rely on observable indicators such as disability classifications and educational placements to allocate resources, yet limited evidence exists regarding whether these indicators correspond to the expenditures districts incur serving students with disabilities. This study examines variation in special education spending across Texas public school districts… more →
authors: David E. DeMatthews, Jinseok Shin, Pedro Reyes

headline: Expanded High-Speed Broadband Internet Access at Home and Student Achievement: Evidence from a Federal Subsidy Program
source: EdWorkingPapers, Annenberg Institute at Brown University
blurb: Policymakers have argued that expanding home broadband would improve educational outcomes. However, prior studies report mixed, null, or negative effects on achievement, with limited post-pandemic evidence. Using district-level achievement and enrollment data from a national broadband subsidy program serving 23 million low-income households, we examine whether increased uptake is associated with… more →
authors: Nicolas Pardo, Jared N. Schachner, Hernan Galperin, François Bar

headline: Policy Landscape of Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education: A Content Analysis of State-Level Policy Guidance Documents
blurb: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in K-12 education has outpaced the development of coherent policy frameworks, raising governance challenges for policymakers. This study examines how U.S. states conceptualize AI governance through qualitative content analysis of policy guidance documents from 40 states and territorial jurisdictions issued between 2023 and 2026. Findings indicate that ethics and data privacy dominate current policy approaches, while equity considerations and educator capacity-building receive moderate attention, and stakeholder trust and ongoing monitoring remain underdeveloped. The study identifies policy gaps and implications for developing more comprehensive and responsible AI governance in K-12 education.

headline: Multiyear Looping and Student Achievement
blurb: Multiyear teacher–student assignments, often known as “looping”, extend relationships among teachers, students, and families beyond a single school year. Using administrative data from a large urban district spanning more than a decade, we develop an empirical approach to identifying intentional looping and estimate its associations with student achievement in grades 4–8, distinguishing looping from incidental repeat teacher–student matches and separating intended from realized continuity. Within a fixed-effects framework that accounts for selection into and out of looping classes, results show that looping is uncommon but associated with gains of roughly 0.04–0.05 standard deviations in ELA and 0.025–0.04 in math—meaningfully larger than those associated with incidental repeat matches. Estimated associations are larger in middle-grade ELA and elementary math and remain robust to alternative model specifications and definitions.

headline: The Chronic(les) of Absenteeism Measurement: Unpacking the Many Measures of Attendance and Evidence for a Lower Chronic Absenteeism Threshold
blurb: This study investigates how absenteeism can be more rigorously measured as an early warning indicator of future academic risk. Using administrative data from 8,891 Boston Public Schools students followed from Pre-K through eighth grade, we (1) describe patterns in excused, unexcused, and total absences, measured as both days and rates, across grades; (2) apply Signal Detection Theory and Receiver… more →
authors: Tiffany Wu, Christina Weiland, Thomas Staines

headline: Remediation or Roadblock? The Effects of Failing Virginia's Accountability Exams
blurb: Virginia’s Standards of Learning (SOL) system requires students to pass end-of-course exams to earn verified credits needed for high school graduation. Scoring below the passing cutoff may create a barrier to completing a high school degree, but it also triggers state-mandated remediation, which may include additional instruction and tutoring. Because these channels push in opposite directions,… more →
authors: Arnav Dharmagadda

headline: Composition, Distribution, and Stability of the Special Education Teacher Workforce in Seven States
blurb: Special education staffing challenges threaten the delivery of effective special education services to students with disabilities. We investigated the composition, distribution, and stability of the special education teacher (SET) workforce over time and across seven states. Some challenges were similar across states, such as trends in SET workforce stability over time, whereas other challenges (e.g., SET certification rates) varied considerably by state. Staffing challenges also varied within some states, contributing to considerable inequity in SET stability and in the distribution of novice SETs, SETs without full certification, and SETs of color. These findings suggest a need for policies and practices that vary by state context and target the districts and schools most affected by SET staffing challenges.

headline: A Broader View of Recovery: Exploring Non-Test Student Outcomes in the Wake of the COVID-19 Pandemic
blurb: The COVID-19 pandemic sharply reduced student test scores, and ESSER-funded academic interventions largely failed to recover those losses. Yet few researchers have examined whether these interventions affected students in ways beyond test scores. We use rich longitudinal data from Guilford County Schools (GCS) to document trends before and after the pandemic in attendance, suspensions, disciplinary referrals, and course grades from 2016-17 through 2023-24. All non-test outcomes worsened in GCS after the pandemic, widening pre-existing gaps by race and school poverty level. We also estimate how participation in GCS’s tutoring and summer school in 2021–22 and 2022–23 affect these non-test outcomes. Students who participated in recovery interventions showed improved attendance and discipline in the following year. Effects varied across interventions: summer school robustly improved attendance the following school year, while tutoring improved discipline in one year (2021–22) and attendance in the other (2022–23). These results demonstrate that academic interventions support students on dimensions beyond traditionally measured academic performance and contribute to recovering student engagement and well-being.
authors: Ian Callen, Elise Dizon-Ross, Dan Goldhaber, Thomas J. Kane, Andrew McEachin, Emily Morton

headline: The Special Education Teacher Pipeline in Pennsylvania: Year 4 Report
blurb: This report summarizes findings from the fourth year of a long-term research partnership on the special education teacher pipeline in Pennsylvania and projects associated with the Bureau of Special Education’s Attract-Prepare-Retain (APR) efforts. We analyzed administrative and survey data associated with eight APR projects and grants that occurred during the 2025–26 school year: Accelerated Program for PK–12 Special Education Teacher Certification Grant, Developing Future Special Educators Grant, APR Mentoring, Networking and Learning Communities, Middle School Learning Institute, World of Learning (WOL) American Sign Language (ASL) courses, Paraeducator Preparation Pathways Grant, and Master’s Level Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP) Stipend for School-Based Placements. The findings build on data from the 2024–25 school year implementation and provide early evidence of project success.
authors: Allison Gilmour, Equia Aniagyei-Cobbold, Marcy Stein

headline: Diverted to What? The Impact of Community College Attendance on Mid-Career Occupational Characteristics and Wages
blurb: We combine data from the NLSY-97 and O*NET to compare the educational attainment, wages, and occupational characteristics of similar (propensity-weighted) two- and four-year starters in their thirties. Consistent with prior research, we find that two-year starters are over 20 percentage points less likely to earn a bachelor's degree than four-year peers. However, we find mixed results on wages. We generally identify under 10 percent differences in two- and four-year starters’ wages, but magnitudes and significance are somewhat sensitive to weighting specification in ways that suggest wage penalties of two-year attendance may be greater for students who more closely resemble typical four-year (rather than two-year) starters. Across specifications, we find that differences in key occupational characteristics are more modest than differences in educational attainment. Two-year starters are about 6 percentage points less likely to work in a job that typically requires a bachelor's degree and hold jobs with similar math, though lower social, skill requirements as four-year peers. Finally, we find that two-year starters more often work in the trades and applied sciences, whereas four-year peers more often work in professions such as teaching. Results highlight a need for more understanding of how college level affects life course trajectories beyond educational attainment.

headline: Less Is More? The Causal Effect of Four-Day School Weeks on Teacher Turnover
blurb: The use of the four-day school week (4dsw) in the United States has expanded rapidly over the past two decades. Previous work examines the impact of 4dsw on student outcomes, but less research to date examines its effect on teachers even though schools in some locales have adopted 4dsw to improve recruitment and retention. This paper uses a difference-in-differences design to estimate the effect of 4dsw adoption in Oregon, a state with early and widespread 4dsw use, on teacher retention in both the short and long term. We find that adopting a four-day week increased turnover among teachers by approximately 2 percentage points overall. These increases are driven by schools that adopted prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and continue to impact schools in the longer term. The findings suggest that policy makers interested in implementing 4dsw for improved teacher retention should exercise caution.
authors: Aaron J. Ainsworth, Yujia Liu, Emily K. Penner

headline: From Middle School to Charter High School: Exploring Curricular Pathways and Postsecondary Education in Texas
blurb: This study examines whether attending a charter high school during the pivotal middle-to-high school transition yields meaningful educational benefits for Texas students who previously graduated from traditional public middle schools. To account for high school mobility, we distinguish charter stayers (who remain in charter high schools) from charter leavers (who return to traditional public schools) and match each group to observationally similar traditional public school (TPS) students (who remain in TPS). Results indicate that charter stayers accumulated more dual-credit coursework and achieved moderately higher standardized exit-exam scores, whereas charter leavers appeared broadly similar to TPS students. In postsecondary outcomes, charter stayers were more likely to enroll on time, attend four-year colleges, and complete degrees earlier, while charter leavers showed little difference in longer-run attainment. These positive associations were concentrated among students attending campus charter high schools, with relatively limited differences for students attending open-enrollment charters.

headline: Unpacking Treatment Effect Heterogeneity in a Large-Scale Dropout-Prevention Experiment
blurb: Timely high school completion is a critical step in successful transitions to post-secondary schooling and the labor market. This randomized controlled trial, deployed in two urban, disadvantaged school districts, tests the effectiveness of a mature and comprehensive student-support program on an unusually large scale (n=2,528). While overall effects on graduation rates are small and… more →
authors: Thomas S. Dee, Chloe R. Gibbs, Rebecca Margolit-Chan, Lillian Morrell, James Sullivan

headline: WEBINAR: Changes Ahead for Head Start: Examining the New Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
blurb: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would overhaul Head Start. FutureEd examines what the proposed rule would change and what it could mean for programs, families, and states. Note that the National Conference of State Legislatures hosts a separate webinar on the same rule on September 24, 2026.

headline: WEBINAR: Postsecondary Pathways | Aligning Education, Correctional Rehabilitation, and Workforce Readiness
blurb: FutureEd hosts a virtual discussion of postsecondary pathways that connect education, correctional rehabilitation, and workforce readiness. Useful for policy staff tracking how college and career programs for incarcerated and reentering students fit together across agencies.

headline: WEBINAR: Homeroom with Education Leaders | From the Ballot to the Policy Agenda: What State Elections Mean for Education
blurb: State election results reshape education agendas well before new laws appear. In this installment of FutureEd's Homeroom with Education Leaders series, panelists consider what recent state elections signal for the policy agenda ahead. A useful briefing for anyone tracking legislative sessions and gubernatorial priorities.

headline: Government Regulation of Nonprofits at a Crossroads: Crafting a Research Agenda for a New Era
blurb: The Urban Institute and Indiana University's Lilly Family School of Philanthropy host an interactive, multidisciplinary working session to identify gaps in what we know about nonprofit-sector regulation and to propose ways to fill them. The resulting proposals will form a public research agenda. Seasoned and new scholars, practitioners, and regulators are all encouraged to register; the Charles Stewart Mott Foundation is supporting the event.

headline: Advanced Technological Education (ATE)
blurb: The National Science Foundation's Advanced Technological Education (ATE) program funds technician education for high-technology fields, centered on two-year institutions and built on partnerships among schools, colleges, industry, and economic development agencies. Support covers curriculum development, faculty and teacher professional development, career pathways, and applied research. Full proposals are due October 1, 2026.

headline: Gaps in State Workforce Priorities, Needs, and Training Programs
blurb: State policymakers rank postsecondary education and workforce development among their top priorities, yet aligning training with labor market demand remains difficult despite federally mandated planning processes meant to foster it. This report analyzes the most recent WIOA plans (Program Years 2024–2027) and eligible training provider (ETP) lists to assess how well states target in-demand, high-quality (IDHQ) occupations and whether training supply meets that demand. We find no shared definition of a credential of value: fifteen plans define the term and only eight set a measurable wage benchmark. Most states target fewer in-demand occupations than they could, and only about one-third of targeted occupations qualify as IDHQ. On average, 47 percent of a state's ETP programs train for at least one IDHQ occupation, and completers fill only about 14 percent of IDHQ openings. ETPs undersupply 90 percent of IDHQ occupations, including licensed practical and vocational nurses, while oversupplying a handful, such as phlebotomists and emergency medical technicians, sometimes by thousands.

headline: Can Early Exposure to the Teaching Profession Increase Teacher Supply and Diversity? New Evidence on the Teacher Pipeline
blurb: We examine whether early exposure to the teaching career has the potential to expand the size and diversity of new teacher supply. Exploiting the staggered expansion of high school education courses across Texas, we find little evidence that these courses increased new teacher supply or diversity despite course takers being substantially more diverse than the teacher workforce. High school education course takers who become teachers are similarly effective and more likely to be retained than their peers. Most course takers drop out of the teacher pipeline prior to college enrollment where racial gaps in 4-year college going serve as major barriers. Our findings suggest that early exposure without support to increase college going is unlikely to increase teacher supply or diversity.

headline: The Lingering Legacy of Redlining on School Funding, Diversity, and Performance
blurb: Historically, the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) “redlined” neighborhoods, systematically disadvantaging low-income and minority communities in the United States. This study examines the enduring legacy of these discriminatory practices on modern public education, analyzing school funding, diversity, and achievement across 144 U.S. statistical areas. We find that the consequences of redlining persist today. Districts with a high concentration of formerly D-graded neighborhoods raise less local revenue and rely disproportionately on state and federal aid. Schools in these areas predominantly educate Black, non-White, and low-income students and post significantly lower average test scores. Because public education draws on neighborhood-based revenue and enrollment, the historic policies that shaped neighborhoods continue to shape educational outcomes today.

headline: Does Civic Education Impact Primary School Students’ Civic Outcomes? Experimental Evidence from Liberia
blurb: We present experimental evidence on a civic education program in Liberia’s public primary schools across 140 schools serving grades 3 and 4. The program provided new civic textbooks, teacher training, twice-weekly instruction, and regular classroom monitoring. After one school year, treatment students scored 0.38 SDs higher on civic knowledge assessments. Gains were concentrated in factual knowledge (0.37 SDs), with positive effects across the achievement distribution. However, the program had no impact on students’ civic engagement. Classroom observation data reveal that instruction was heavily textbook-centered, in contrast to the participatory models common in high-income countries.

headline: Special Rule 505 of Title V: Sustaining Separate and Unequal Funding Between Historically Black and Historically White Emerging HSIs

Drawing on interviews, policy texts, and institutional artifacts, the study explores the tensions between historic missions of racial uplift and contemporary demands for inclusive excellence within a politically regressive policy context. Using a critical organizational lens grounded in anti-colonial theory and isomorphism, findings reveal how educators resist and reinterpret coercive and memetic pressures shaping institutional identity. Despite exclusion from Title V funding under Special Rule 505, Hispanic-serving HBCUs demonstrate Afro-centric servingness aligned with Title III and V priorities, exposing racialized inequities while highlighting agency in advancing anti-colonial practices.

headline: Unequal Foundations: Racial Disparities in School Building Conditions in New York State
blurb: School infrastructure is a critical yet often overlooked factor shaping student health, learning, and well-being. This study examines racial disparities in public school building conditions across New York State using building inspection data linked to demographic and fiscal data. Schools serving more students of color are significantly more likely to have poor overall conditions, inadequate ventilation, mold exposure, and reduced access to athletic fields, gymnasiums, and health offices. A Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition shows that local property taxes are the largest contributor to racial gaps in building quality, while progressive state building aid helps reduce these disparities. These findings highlight persistent infrastructure inequities and the need for targeted investments to ensure all students have access to safe and healthy learning environments.

headline: The Reliability of Classroom Observations and Student Surveys in Non-Research Settings: Evidence From a Middle-Income Country
blurb: We present one of the first Generalizability studies of non-test measures of teaching effectiveness administered by practitioners in a middle-income country. The reliability of observations varies widely (from 0 to 0.75 on a 0–1 scale) and depends upon their context (whether they are conducted during training or on the job) and rater assignment configurations. The reliability of surveys varies substantially, coinciding with a change in the students sampled across occasions. Our estimates of reliabilty are comparable to those from research in high-income countries, but the variation within our estimates and between them and those from individual studies suggests that practitioners should conduct their own reliability analyses. We offer guidance on leveraging such analyses to improve the reliability of their measures.

headline: The Effects of the Four-Day School Week on Teacher Recruitment and Retention
blurb: School districts across the United States are increasingly adopting the four-day school week, often in the hope of addressing teacher staffing challenges. We examine the effects of the four-day week on teacher recruitment and retention in Missouri, where 3 in 10 districts currently use it. After presenting qualitative data showing that educators believe the four-day week improves recruitment and retention, we estimate the effects of the four-day week on these outcomes using difference-in-differences models. We find no evidence that the four-day school week improves teacher retention or that districts expand their workforce post adoption, though the composition of new hires shifts toward more experienced teachers. We show that our findings are unlikely to be driven by saturation effects.

headline: Approximating the Equilibrium Effects of Informed School Choice
blurb: We study how information about school quality affects families’ choices and how scaling up the intervention changes its impact. In a randomized trial in Chile, we offer families a short video and a personalized school report card before they enroll their children. Treated families choose schools with higher test scores and value added. Among families reached before enrollment, treated children score about 0.2 standard deviations higher in fourth grade, with positive but less precise estimates on later assessments. We embed the experimentally identified demand shift in a structural model of school choice and competition to study equilibrium effects at scale. Capacity constraints and centralized assignment attenuate the demand-side gains, but the same shift in demand strengthens schools’ incentives to improve quality, and the supply response roughly offsets the congestion effect. More generally, equilibrium scaling can alter experimental effects in either direction because congestion and endogenous quality responses work against each other. We use the model to guide the design of a follow-up cluster-randomized experiment, focusing on the tradeoff between precision and contamination from equilibrium spillovers.
authors: Claudia Allende, Francisco Gallego, Christopher Neilson

headline: Targeted Acceleration in Middle School Math: Impacts on College Entry, Degree Completion, and STEM
blurb: We study an accelerated 3-year math curriculum offered in the middle schools of a large urban district that enables students to finish Algebra I and Geometry before high school. Entry to the program is based on 5th-grade math test scores, with a cutoff at the 80th percentile. Continuing eligibility requires at least a B grade in the previous year; successful completion of all three years is highly correlated with an index of non-cognitive skills. Following students for 6 years after high school graduation, we find that the impacts of admission vary widely by non-cognitive skill and gender. Marginally eligible boys with high non-cognitive skills have a 33 percentage point (ppt.) increase in the probability of completing calculus by 11th grade and a 12 ppt. increase in the probability of completing a major in STEM or business within 6 years; boys with lower noncognitive skills take more advanced math classes in high school but have no significant effects on their college outcomes. Like their male peers, marginally eligible girls with high non-cognitive skills are more likely to complete calculus by 11th grade (+17 ppt.). Their rate of graduating with a STEM or business major is unaffected, but they switch from social sciences to the core STEM majors (science, engineering and math). Girls in the two lower terciles of non-cognitive skill are also strongly affected by entry to the program, with higher participation in advanced math classes in high school, higher rates of entry to selective 4-year colleges, and higher rates of completing a STEM or business major (+12 ppt).
authors: David Card, Laura Giuliano

headline: Education and Climate Change: Synthesizing the Evidence to Guide Future Research
blurb: Schools are both vulnerable to climate change and uniquely positioned to be part of the solution. We conduct an integrative review of interdisciplinary research and data to better understand the bidirectional relationship between education systems and our changing climate. We identify and describe the challenges, opportunities, and areas for future research for five interrelated dimensions: (a) the effects of climate change on school infrastructure, budgets, and operations; (b) the effects of climate and environmental pressures on child development and students’ success in school; (c) the effects of education systems on the environment; (d) teaching climate science, nature-based education, traditional ecological knowledge, and career and technical education for jobs that advance sustainable practices; and (e) the role of schools in advancing community-wide efforts for resilience and sustainability.
