headline: Full-Day Kindergarten and Enrollment Patterns: Evidence from Massachusetts
blurb: Public school districts across the United States face persistent enrollment pressures. Birth rates have declined and school choice has expanded for more than a decade, and enrollment losses deepened sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic. These trends carry direct consequences for funding, staffing, and school viability. This paper examines whether full-day kindergarten (FDK) can serve as a policy lever to attract and retain public school students, using a staggered difference-in-differences design applied to Massachusetts’ FDK expansion. FDK implementation increases public kindergarten enrollment by approximately 9%, about 20 additional students per district, a net gain that conversion from half-day programs alone cannot explain, though where these students come from remains an open question our data cannot resolve. Positive enrollment effects persist through grade 3, consistent with FDK building some lasting attachment to public schools rather than a temporary enrollment boost. Beyond its well-documented benefits for children and families, FDK may offer districts one additional tool for stabilizing enrollment, though its value as such depends on weighing these gains against implementation costs.
authors: Mingyan Ma, Abigail Francis

headline: Navigating Conflicting Pressures: How Districts Spend Federal COVID-19 Relief Funds
blurb: Federal COVID-19 relief funds provided a large increase in school district revenue, with fewer requirements than usual. Districts received widespread criticism, based on little systematic evidence, for spending federal funds slowly or ineffectively. Institutional theories predict a common response to funds across districts, while other theories predict variation in use of these funds. How have districts used this rare funding increase and how has that varied by state or district context? We use district-level spending data 2010-2023 to examine spending changes and superintendent interviews in four states (KS, MI, OK, RI) to understand district leaders’ rationales for spending changes. We find that spending increased within three years, with larger increases in high-poverty districts, consistent with the distribution of relief funds. Adjusting for differences in federal funding increases, changes in spending are similar across contexts. Interviews reveal that districts across contexts used funds to implement instructional programs, seeking effective ways to improve student learning while gathering data to document effectiveness for local stakeholders. District leaders navigate conflicting pressures, prioritizing student learning while anticipating future accountability requirements, documenting spending effectiveness, avoiding a fiscal cliff, and communicating with communities. District leaders face similar conflicting pressures and adopt similar spending approaches across contexts.
authors: Emily Rauscher, Daniel R. Alvord, Jordan Mosby

headline: Does Better Academic Preparation Predict Teacher Workforce Outcomes?

Teachers who expressed interest in education at university application are more likely to remain in the workforce once they enter.

headline: Sidewalks for Students: Google Street View Measures of Walkability Around Schools and Chronic Absenteeism Rates
blurb: This study brings together ideas from education, public health, and urban planning to assess whether the walkability of the built environment around schools is related to their chronic absenteeism rates. We use national data from the 2018–2019 NCES Common Core of Data and the Office of Civil Rights and computer vision-derived estimates of the physical environment captured in Google Street View Images. We compare schools in the same district to one another and find that schools with a higher proportion of images with sidewalks and streetlights within 1 mile of their location tend to have lower chronic absenteeism rates. These findings support the idea that physical infrastructure can be an important structural barrier to attendance.
authors: Julia Burdick-Will, Michael D.M. Bader, Quynh C. Nguyen

Parents weighed instructional approach, belonging, safety, diversity, and social-emotional support above traditional academic metrics, and relationships with teachers and principals shaped their decisions. headline: The Pipeline of Alternative Teacher Certification: Evaluating iteach
blurb: This report evaluates iteach, one of the country’s largest alternative teacher certification providers, by tracing candidates through the full pipeline, from application to classroom outcomes, primarily across Texas, Louisiana, and Virginia. Drawing on program records alongside Texas state employment and evaluation data, the analysis follows who applies and enrolls, who completes, who stays in teaching, and how effective those teachers are. Application volume has grown sharply since 2015, and enrolled candidates skew well older than the “recent graduate” stereotype, with most aged 30 or older and many entering from school-adjacent or mid-career roles. The content-area certification exam emerges as the central pre-hire bottleneck, the stage at which candidates of color narrow most sharply. Among completers, retention exceeds Texas peer benchmarks and widens with tenure, roughly four in five earn Accomplished or Distinguished evaluation ratings, and student-growth outcomes sit near the state average.
authors: Andrew Kwok, Brendan Bartanen, Kate Barnes
